  The analysis of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{gather}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} is identical.
  Notice that, if Case~1 occurs during the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} method, then
  only one node, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_r$ has the size of its block changed. Therefore,
  at most one node, namely $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_r$, goes from being rugged to being
  fragile.  If Case~2 occurs, then a new node is created, and this node
  is fragile, but no other node changes size, so the number of fragile
  nodes increases by one.  Thus, in either Case~1 or Case~2 the potential
  of the SEList increases by at most one.
  Finally, if Case~3 occurs, it is because $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}}-1}$
  are all fragile nodes.  Then $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{spread}(}u_0\ensuremath{)}$ is called and these \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}}
  fragile nodes are replaced with $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}}+1$ rugged nodes.  Finally, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}
  is added to $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_0$'s block, making $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_0$ fragile.  In total the
  potential decreases by $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}}-1$.

  Each time Case~1 or Case~2 occurs, the potential increases by at

  The potential (which counts the number of fragile nodes) is never
  less than 0.  We conclude that, for every occurrence of Case~3, there

Ignoring the cost of calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{spread}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{gather}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}}, an SEList with block size \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}} supports the operations \begin{itemize} \item \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{get}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{set}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} in $O(1+\min\{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}},\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}-\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}\}/\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}})$ time per operation; and \item \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} in $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}}+\min\{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}},\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}-\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}\}/\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}})$ time per operation. \end{itemize} Furthermore, beginning with an empty SEList, any sequence of $m$ \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} operations results in a total of $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}}m)$ time spent during all calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{spread}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{gather}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}}. The space (measured in words)\footnote{Recall \secref{model} for a discussion of how memory is measured.} used by an SEList that stores \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} elements is $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} +O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}} + \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}})$.
Recall \secref{model} for a discussion of how memory is measured.

content: The SEList is a trade-off between an ArrayList and a DLList where the relative mix of these two structures depends on the block size \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}}. At the extreme $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}}=2$, each SEList node stores at most three values, which is not much different than a DLList. At the other extreme, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{b}}}}>\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}$, all the elements are stored in a single array, just like in an ArrayList. In between these two extremes lies a trade-off between the time it takes to add or remove a list item and the time it takes to locate a particular list item.

content: Both singly-linked and doubly-linked lists are established techniques, having been used in programs for over 40 years. They are discussed, for example, by Knuth \cite[Sections~2.2.3--2.2.5]{k97v1}. Even the SEList data structure seems to be a well-known data structures exercise. The SEList is sometimes referred to as an \emph{unrolled linked list} \cite{sra94}. \index{unrolled linked list|seealso{SEList}} \index{linked list!unrolled|seealso{SEList}} Another way to save space in a doubly-linked list is to use so-called XOR-lists. \index{XOR-list} In an XOR-list, each node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, contains only one pointer, called \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{nextprev}}}}, that holds the bitwise exclusive-or of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{prev}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}}}. The list itself needs to store two pointers, one to the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{dummy}}}} node and one to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{dummy}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}}} (the first node, or \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{dummy}}}} if the list is empty). This technique uses the fact that, if we have pointers to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{prev}}}}, then we can extract \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}}} using the formula

content: Why is it not possible to use a dummy node in an SLList to avoid all the special cases that occur in the operations \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{push}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{pop}()}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}()}}?

Design and implement an SLList method, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{second\_last}()}}, that returns the second-last element of an SLList. Do this without using the member variable, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}, that keeps track of the size of the list.

Implement the List operations \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{get}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{set}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} on an SLList. Each of these operations should run in $O(1+\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}})$ time.

Design and implement an SLList method, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{reverse}()}} that reverses the order of elements in an SLList. This method should run in $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$ time, should not use recursion, should not use any secondary data structures, and should not create any new nodes.

Design and implement SLList and DLList methods called \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{check\_size}()}}. These methods walk through the list and count the number of nodes to see if this matches the value, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}, stored in the list. These methods return nothing, but throw an exception if the size they compute does not match the value of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}.

content: Write a DLList method, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{absorb}(\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}})}}, that takes as an argument a DLList, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}}, empties it and appends its contents, in order, to the receiver. For example, if \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} contains $a,b,c$ and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} contains $d,e,f$, then after calling \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}.\mathrm{absorb}(\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} will contain $a,b,c,d,e,f$ and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} will be empty.

Write a method \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{deal}()}} that removes all the elements with odd-numbered indices from a DLList and return a DLList containing these elements. For example, if \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}}, contains the elements $a,b,c,d,e,f$, then after calling \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}.\mathrm{deal}()}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} should contain $a,c,e$ and a list containing $b,d,f$ should be returned.

\exclabel{dllist-sort} \index{merge-sort} This exercise walks you through an implementation of the merge-sort algorithm for sorting a DLList, as discussed in \secref{merge-sort}. \javaonly{In your implementation, perform comparisons between elements using the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{compare\_to}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} method so that the resulting implementation can sort any DLList containing elements that implement the Comparable interface.} \begin{enumerate} \item Write a DLList method called \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{take\_first}(\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}})}}. This method takes the first node from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} and appends it to the the receiving list. This is equivalent to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\mathrm{size}(),\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}.\mathrm{remove}(0)})}, except that it should not create a new node. \item Write a DLList static method, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{merge}(\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}},\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}})}}, that takes two sorted lists \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}}, merges them, and returns a new sorted list containing the result. This causes \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} to be emptied in the proces. For example, if \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} contains $a,c,d$ and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} contains $b,e,f$, then this method returns a new list containing $a,b,c,d,e,f$. \item Write a DLList method \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{sort}()}} that sorts the elements contained in the list using the merge sort algorithm. This recursive algorithm works in the following way: \begin{enumerate} \item If the list contains 0 or 1 elements then there is nothing to do. Otherwise, \item Using the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{truncate}(\mathrm{size}()/2})} method, split the list into two lists of approximately equal length, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}}; \item Recursively sort \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}}; \item Recursively sort \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}}; and, finally, \item Merge \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} into a single sorted list. \end{enumerate} \end{enumerate}

\begin{exc}\exclabel{dllist-sort}
  \index{merge-sort}%
  This exercise walks you through an implementation of the merge-sort
  algorithm for sorting a DLList, as discussed in \secref{merge-sort}.
  \javaonly{In your implementation, perform comparisons between elements
  using the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{compare\_to}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} method so that the resulting implementation can
  sort any DLList containing elements that implement the Comparable
  interface.}
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item Write a DLList method called \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{take\_first}(\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}})}}.
       This method takes the first node from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} and appends it to the the
       receiving list.  This is equivalent to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\mathrm{size}(),\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}.\mathrm{remove}(0)})},
       except that it should not create a new node.
    \item Write a DLList static method, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{merge}(\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}},\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}})}}, that takes two
       sorted lists \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}}, merges them, and returns a new sorted
       list containing the result.  This causes \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} to be emptied
       in the proces.  For example, if \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} contains $a,c,d$ and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} contains
       $b,e,f$, then this method returns a new list containing $a,b,c,d,e,f$.
    \item Write a DLList method \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{sort}()}} that sorts the elements
       contained in the list using the merge sort algorithm.
       This recursive algorithm works in the following way:
       \begin{enumerate}
          \item If the list contains 0 or 1 elements then there is
            nothing to do.  Otherwise,
          \item Using the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{truncate}(\mathrm{size}()/2})} method, split the list
            into two lists of approximately equal length, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}};
          \item Recursively sort \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}};
          \item Recursively sort \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}}; and, finally,
          \item Merge \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_1}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{l_2}}}} into a single sorted list.
       \end{enumerate}
  \end{enumerate}
\end{exc}

content: The efficiency of skiplists relies on their use of randomization. When a new element is added to a skiplist, the skiplist uses random coin tosses to determine the height of the new element. The performance of skiplists is expressed in terms of expected running times and path lengths. This expectation is taken over the random coin tosses used by the skiplist. In the implementation, the random coin tosses used by a skiplist are simulated using a pseudo-random number (or bit) generator.

content: \index{skiplist} Conceptually, a skiplist is a sequence of singly-linked lists $L_0,\ldots,L_h$. Each list $L_r$ contains a subset of the items in $L_{r-1}$. We start with the input list $L_0$ that contains \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} items and construct $L_1$ from $L_0$, $L_2$ from $L_1$, and so on. The items in $L_r$ are obtained by tossing a coin for each element, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, in $L_{r-1}$ and including \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} in $L_r$ if the coin turns up as heads. This process ends when we create a list $L_r$ that is empty. An example of a skiplist is shown in \figref{skiplist}.

content: For an element, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, in a skiplist, we call the \emph{height} \index{height!of a skiplist} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} the largest value $r$ such that \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} appears in $L_r$. Thus, for example, elements that only appear in $L_0$ have height $0$. If we spend a few moments thinking about it, we notice that the height of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} corresponds to the following experiment: Toss a coin repeatedly until it comes up as tails. How many times did it come up as heads? The answer, not surprisingly, is that the expected height of a node is 1. (We expect to toss the coin twice before getting tails, but we don't count the last toss.) The \emph{height} of a skiplist is the height of its tallest node. At the head of every list is a special node, called the \emph{sentinel}, \index{sentinel node} that acts as a dummy node for the list. The key property of skiplists is that there is a short path, called the \emph{search path}, \index{search path!in a skiplist} from the sentinel in $L_h$ to every node in $L_0$. Remembering how to construct a search path for a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, is easy (see \figref{skiplist-searchpath}) : Start at the top left corner of your skiplist (the sentinel in $L_h$) and always go right unless that would overshoot \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, in which case you should take a step down into the list below. More precisely, to construct the search path for the node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} in $L_0$, we start at the sentinel, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}, in $L_h$. Next, we examine \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}}}. If \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}}} contains an item that appears before \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} in $L_0$, then we set $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}}}$. Otherwise, we move down and continue the search at the occurrence of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}} in the list $L_{h-1}$. We continue this way until we reach the predecessor of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} in $L_0$.

To implement the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} method in a SkiplistSSet we search for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} and then splice \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} into a few lists $L_0$,\ldots,$L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{k}}}}}$, where \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{k}}}} is selected using the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{pick\_height}()}} method. The easiest way to do this is to use an array, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{stack}}}}, that keeps track of the nodes at which the search path goes down from some list $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ into $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}-1}$. More precisely, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{stack}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}]}} is the node in $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ where the search path proceeded down into $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}-1}$. The nodes that we modify to insert \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} are precisely the nodes $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{stack}}[0]}},\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{stack}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{k}}]}}$. The following code implements this algorithm for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}: \label{pg:skiplist-add}

\begin{flushleft}
\hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}} \gets  \ensuremath{sentinel}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}} \gets  \ensuremath{h}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} {\color{black} \textbf{while}} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}} \ge 0} {\color{black} \textbf{do}} \\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} {\color{black} \textbf{while}} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}] \ne nil} {\color{black} \textbf{and}} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}].\ensuremath{\mathit{x}} < x} {\color{black} \textbf{do}} \\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}} \gets  \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}]}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} {\color{black} \textbf{if}} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}] \ne nil} {\color{black} \textbf{and}} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}].\ensuremath{\mathit{x}} \eq x} {\color{black} \textbf{then}}  {\color{black} \textbf{return}} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{false}}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{stack}}[\ensuremath{r}] \gets  \ensuremath{u}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}} \gets  \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}} - 1}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}} \gets  \ensuremath{\mathrm{new\_node}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}, \mathrm{pick\_height}()})}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} {\color{black} \textbf{while}} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}} < \ensuremath{\mathit{w}}.\mathrm{height}()} {\color{black} \textbf{do}} \\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}} \gets  \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}} + 1}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{stack}}[\ensuremath{h}] \gets  \ensuremath{sentinel}   }\ {\color{comment}\# height increased}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} {\color{black} \textbf{for}} \ensuremath{i} {\color{black} \textbf{in}} \ensuremath{0,1,2,\ldots,\mathrm{len}(\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}})-1} {\color{black} \textbf{do}} \\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}.\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}] \gets  \ensuremath{\mathit{stack}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}].\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{stack}}[\ensuremath{i}].\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}] \gets  w}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}} \gets  \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}} + 1}}\\
\hspace*{1em} \hspace*{1em} {\color{black} \textbf{return}} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{true}}}\\
\end{flushleft}

content: \seclabel{skiplistlist} \index{SkiplistList@SkiplistList} A SkiplistList implements the List interface using a skiplist structure. In a SkiplistList, $L_0$ contains the elements of the list in the order in which they appear in the list. As in a SkiplistSSet, elements can be added, removed, and accessed in $O(\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$ time. For this to be possible, we need a way to follow the search path for the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}th element in $L_0$. The easiest way to do this is to define the notion of the \emph{length} of an edge in some list, $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$. We define the length of every edge in $L_{0}$ as 1. The length of an edge, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e}}}}, in $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}>0$, is defined as the sum of the lengths of the edges below \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e}}}} in $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}-1}$. Equivalently, the length of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e}}}} is the number of edges in $L_0$ below \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e}}}}. See \figref{skiplist-lengths} for an example of a skiplist with the lengths of its edges shown. Since the edges of skiplists are stored in arrays, the lengths can be stored the same way:

content: The useful property of this definition of length is that, if we are currently at a node that is at position \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} in $L_0$ and we follow an edge of length $\ell$, then we move to a node whose position, in $L_0$, is $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}+\ell$. In this way, while following a search path, we can keep track of the position, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}, of the current node in $L_0$. When at a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, in $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$, we go right if \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} plus the length of the edge \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}]}} is less than \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}. Otherwise, we go down into $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}-1}$.

Since the hardest part of the operations \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{get}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{set}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} is finding the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}th node in $L_0$, these operations run in $O(\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$ time. Adding an element to a SkiplistList at a position, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, is fairly simple. Unlike in a SkiplistSSet, we are sure that a new node will actually be added, so we can do the addition at the same time as we search for the new node's location. We first pick the height, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{k}}}}, of the newly inserted node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}, and then follow the search path for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}. Any time the search path moves down from $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ with $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}\le \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{k}}}}$, we splice \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}} into $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$. \seclabel{skiplist-analysis}
In this section, we analyze the expected height, size, and length of
the search path in a skiplist.  This section requires a background in
basic probability.  Several proofs are based on the following basic
observation about coin tosses.

content: \lemlabel{coin-tosses} \index{coin toss} Let $T$ be the number of times a fair coin is tossed up to and including the first time the coin comes up heads. Then $\E[T]=2$.

Suppose we stop tossing the coin the first time it comes up heads. Define the indicator variable \[ I_{i} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0 & \mbox{if the coin is tossed less than $i$ times} \\ 1 & \mbox{if the coin is tossed $i$ or more times} \end{array}\right. \] Note that $I_i=1$ if and only if the first $i-1$ coin tosses are tails, so $\E[I_i]=\Pr\{I_i=1\}=1/2^{i-1}$. Observe that $T$, the total number of coin tosses, can be written as $T=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} I_i$. Therefore, \begin{align*} \E[T] & = \E\left[\sum_{i=1}^\infty I_i\right] \\ & = \sum_{i=1}^\infty \E\left[I_i\right] \\ & = \sum_{i=1}^\infty 1/2^{i-1} \\ & = 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + \cdots \\ & = 2 \enspace . \qedhere \end{align*}

\begin{align*}
    \E[T] & =  \E\left[\sum_{i=1}^\infty I_i\right] \\
     & =  \sum_{i=1}^\infty \E\left[I_i\right] \\
     & =  \sum_{i=1}^\infty 1/2^{i-1} \\
     & =  1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + \cdots \\
     & =  2 \enspace .   \qedhere
  \end{align*}

The probability that any particular element, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, is included in list $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ is $1/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$, so the expected number of nodes in $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ is $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$.\footnote{See \secref{randomization} to see how this is derived using indicator variables and linearity of expectation.} Therefore, the total expected number of nodes in all lists is \[ \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^\infty \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} = \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}(1+1/2+1/4+1/8+\cdots) = 2\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} \enspace . \qedhere \]
See \secref{randomization} to see how this is derived using indicator variables and linearity of expectation.

content: \lemlabel{skiplist-height} The expected height of a skiplist containing \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} elements is at most $\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + 2$.

For each $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}\in\{1,2,3,\ldots,\infty\}$, define the indicator random variable \[ I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0 & \mbox{if $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ is empty} \\ 1 & \mbox{if $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ is non-empty} \end{array}\right. \] The height, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}, of the skiplist is then given by \[ \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}} = \sum_{r=1}^\infty I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \enspace . \] Note that $I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ is never more than the length, $|L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}|$, of $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$, so \[ \E[I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \le \E[|L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}|] = \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \enspace . \] Therefore, we have \begin{align*} \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] &= \E\left[\sum_{r=1}^\infty I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}\right] \\ &= \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=1}^{\infty} E[I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \\ &= \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=1}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} E[I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] + \sum_{r=\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} E[I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \\ &\le \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=1}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} 1 + \sum_{r=\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\ &\le \log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^\infty 1/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\ &= \log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + 2 \enspace . \qedhere \end{align*}

\begin{proof}
  For each $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}\in\{1,2,3,\ldots,\infty\}$, 
  define the indicator random variable
  \[ I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
     0 & \mbox{if $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ is empty} \\
     1 & \mbox{if $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ is non-empty}
     \end{array}\right.
  \]
  The height, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}, of the skiplist is then given by
  \[
       \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}} = \sum_{r=1}^\infty I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \enspace .
  \]
  Note that $I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ is never more than the length, $|L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}|$, of $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$, so 
  \[
     \E[I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \le \E[|L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}|] = \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \enspace .
  \]
  Therefore, we have
  \begin{align*}
       \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] &= \E\left[\sum_{r=1}^\infty I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}\right] \\
        &= \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=1}^{\infty} E[I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \\
        &= \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=1}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} E[I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}]
                 + \sum_{r=\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} E[I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}]  \\
        &\le \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=1}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} 1
                 + \sum_{r=\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\
        &\le \log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}
                 + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^\infty 1/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\
        &= \log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + 2 \enspace . \qedhere
  \end{align*}
\end{proof}

content: \lemlabel{skiplist-size2} The expected number of nodes in a skiplist containing $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}$ elements, including all occurrences of the sentinel, is $2\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}+O(\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$.

By \lemref{skiplist-size1}, the expected number of nodes, not including the sentinel, is $2\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}$. The number of occurrences of the sentinel is equal to the height, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}$, of the skiplist so, by \lemref{skiplist-height} the expected number of occurrences of the sentinel is at most $\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}+2 = O(\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$.

content: The expected length of a search path in a skiplist is at most $2\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + O(1)$.

The easiest way to see this is to consider the \emph{reverse search path} for a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}. This path starts at the predecessor of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} in $L_0$. At any point in time, if the path can go up a level, then it does. If it cannot go up a level then it goes left. Thinking about this for a few moments will convince us that the reverse search path for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} is identical to the search path for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, except that it is reversed. The number of nodes that the reverse search path visits at a particular level, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}, is related to the following experiment: Toss a coin. If the coin comes up as heads, then move up and stop. Otherwise, move left and repeat the experiment. The number of coin tosses before the heads represents the number of steps to the left that a reverse search path takes at a particular level.\footnote{Note that this might overcount the number of steps to the left, since the experiment should end either at the first heads or when the search path reaches the sentinel, whichever comes first. This is not a problem since the lemma is only stating an upper bound.} \lemref{coin-tosses} tells us that the expected number of coin tosses before the first heads is 1. Let $S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ denote the number of steps the forward search path takes at level $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}$ that go to the right. We have just argued that $\E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}]\le 1$. Furthermore, $S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}\le |L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}|$, since we can't take more steps in $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ than the length of $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$, so \[ \E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \le \E[|L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}|] = \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \enspace . \] We can now finish as in the proof of \lemref{skiplist-height}. Let $S$ be the length of the search path for some node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, in a skiplist, and let $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}$ be the height of the skiplist. Then \begin{align*} \E[S] &= \E\left[ \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}} + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^\infty S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \right] \\ &= \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^\infty \E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \\ &= \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} \E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor+1}^\infty \E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \\ &\le \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} 1 + \sum_{r=\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor+1}^\infty \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\ &\le \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} 1 + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\infty} 1/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\ &\le \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} 1 + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\infty} 1/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\ &\le \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + 3 \\ &\le 2\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + 5 \enspace . \qedhere \end{align*}

  this for a few moments will convince us that the reverse search path for
  \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} is identical to the search path for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, except that it is reversed.
  The number of nodes that the reverse search path visits at a particular
  level, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}, is related to the following experiment:  Toss a coin.
  If the coin comes up as heads, then move up and stop. Otherwise, move
  left and repeat the experiment.  The number of coin tosses before
  the heads represents the number of steps to the left that a reverse
  search path takes at a particular level.\footnote{Note that this
  might overcount the number of steps to the left, since the experiment
  should end either at the first heads or when the search path reaches
  the sentinel, whichever comes first. This is not a problem since the

  that the expected number of coin tosses before the first heads is 1.
  Let $S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ denote the number of steps the forward search path takes at level
  $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}$ that go to the right.   We have just argued that $\E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}]\le
  1$.  Furthermore, $S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}\le |L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}|$, since we can't take more steps
  in $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$ than the length of $L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}$, so
  \[
    \E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \le \E[|L_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}|] = \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \enspace .
  \]
  We can now finish as in the proof of \lemref{skiplist-height}.
  Let $S$ be  the length of the search path for some node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, in a
  skiplist, and let $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}$ be the height of the skiplist.  Then
  \begin{align*}
      \E[S] 
         &= \E\left[ \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}} + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^\infty S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \right] \\
         &= \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^\infty \E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}]  \\
         &= \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} \E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] 
              + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor+1}^\infty \E[S_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}}] \\
         &\le \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} 1
              + \sum_{r=\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor+1}^\infty \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\
         &\le \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} 1
              + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\infty} 1/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\
         &\le \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\lfloor\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\rfloor} 1
              + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}=0}^{\infty} 1/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}} \\
         &\le \E[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{h}}}}] + \log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + 3 \\
         &\le 2\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + 5  \enspace . \qedhere
  \end{align*}
\end{proof}

content: A skiplist containing $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}$ elements has expected size $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$ and the expected length of the search path for any particular element is at most $2\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} + O(1)$.

content: Skiplists were introduced by Pugh \cite{p91} who also presented a number of applications and extensions of skiplists \cite{p89}. Since then they have been studied extensively. Several researchers have done very precise analyses of the expected length and variance of the length of the search path for the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}th element in a skiplist \cite{kp94,kmp95,pmp92}. Deterministic versions \cite{mps92}, biased versions \cite{bbg02,esss01}, and self-adjusting versions \cite{bdl08} of skiplists have all been developed. Skiplist implementations have been written for various languages and frameworks and have been used in open-source database systems \cite{skipdb,redis}. A variant of skiplists is used in the HP-UX operating system kernel's process management structures \cite{hpux}.

content: \index{finger} \index{finger search!in a skiplist} A \emph{finger} in a skiplist is an array that stores the sequence of nodes on a search path at which the search path goes down. (The variable \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{stack}}}} in the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} code on page~\pageref{pg:skiplist-add} is a finger; the shaded nodes in \figref{skiplist-add} show the contents of the finger.) One can think of a finger as pointing out the path to a node in the lowest list, $L_0$. A \emph{finger search} implements the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation using a finger, by walking up the list using the finger until reaching a node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} such that $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} < \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}$ and $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}}}=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}}$ or $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{next}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} > \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}$ and then performing a normal search for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} starting from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. It is possible to prove that the expected number of steps required for a finger search is $O(1+\log r)$, where $r$ is the number values in $L_0$ between \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} and the value pointed to by the finger. Implement a subclass of Skiplist called SkiplistWithFinger that implements \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operations using an internal finger. This subclass stores a finger, which is then used so that every \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation is implemented as a finger search. During each \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation the finger is updated so that each \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation uses, as a starting point, a finger that points to the result of the previous \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation.

content: \chaplabel{hashtables} \chaplabel{hashing} Hash tables are an efficient method of storing a small number, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}, of integers from a large range $U=\{0,\ldots,2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}-1\}$. The term \emph{hash table} \index{hash table} includes a broad range of data structures. The first part of this chapter focuses on two of the most common implementations of hash tables: hashing with chaining and linear probing. Very often hash tables store types of data that are not integers. In this case, an integer \emph{hash code} \index{hash code} is associated with each data item and is used in the hash table. The second part of this chapter discusses how such hash codes are generated. Some of the methods used in this chapter require random choices of integers in some specific range. In the code samples, some of these ``random'' integers are hard-coded constants. These constants were obtained using random bits generated from atmospheric noise.

Let $S$ be the (multi-)set of elements stored in the hash table that are not equal to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}. For an element $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}\in S$, define the indicator variable \[ I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 1 & \mbox{if $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{hash}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{hash}(\ensuremath{\mathit{y}})}}$} \\ 0 & \mbox{otherwise} \end{array}\right. \] and notice that, by \lemref{universal-hashing}, $\E[I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}}] \le 2/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{d}}}}}=2/\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}$. The expected length of the list \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}[\mathrm{hash}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})]}} is given by \begin{eqnarray*} \E\left[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}[\mathrm{hash}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})].\mathrm{size}()}}\right] &=& \E\left[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}} + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}\in S} I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}}\right] \\ &=& \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}} + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}\in S} \E [I_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}} ] \\ &\le& \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}} + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}\in S} 2/\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}} \\ &\le& \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}} + \sum_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}\in S} 2/\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} \\ &\le& \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}} + (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}-\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}})2/\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} \\ &\le& \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}} + 2 \enspace , \end{eqnarray*} as required.

  for some integer $k$.  Thinking in terms of binary numbers, we have

  \]

The following theorem summarizes the performance of a ChainedHashTable
data structure:

content: \thmlabel{hashtable} A ChainedHashTable implements the USet interface. Ignoring the cost of calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{grow}()}}, a ChainedHashTable supports the operations \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} in $O(1)$ expected time per operation. Furthermore, beginning with an empty ChainedHashTable, any sequence of $m$ \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operations results in a total of $O(m)$ time spent during all calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{grow}()}}.

\begin{thm}\thmlabel{hashtable}
  A ChainedHashTable implements the USet interface.  Ignoring the cost of
  calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{grow}()}}, a ChainedHashTable supports the operations \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}},
  \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} in $O(1)$ expected time per operation.
  Furthermore, beginning with an empty ChainedHashTable, any sequence of
  $m$ \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operations results in a total of $O(m)$
  time spent during all calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{grow}()}}.
\end{thm}

That is, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} is equal to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} plus the number of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{del}}}} values in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}. To make this work efficiently, we need \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} to be considerably larger than \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}, so that there are lots of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}} values in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}. content: The correctness of the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} methods is easy to verify, though it relies on the use of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{del}}}} values. Notice that none of these operations ever sets a non-\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}} entry to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}}. Therefore, when we reach an index \ensuremath{\ensuremath{i}'} such that \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}[\ensuremath{i}']\gets \ensuremath{nil}}}, this is a proof that the element, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, that we are searching for is not stored in the table; \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}']}} has always been \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}}, so there is no reason that a previous \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation would have proceeded beyond index \ensuremath{\ensuremath{i}'}. The \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} method works like the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} methods in other array-based data structures. We find the smallest non-negative integer \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{d}}}} such that $2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{d}}}}} \ge 3\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}$. We reallocate the array \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} so that it has size $2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{d}}}}}$, and then we insert all the elements in the old version of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} into the newly-resized copy of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}. While doing this, we reset \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} equal to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} since the newly-allocated \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} contains no \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{del}}}} values.

content: Notice that each operation, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, or \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, finishes as soon as (or before) it discovers the first \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}} entry in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}. The intuition behind the analysis of linear probing is that, since at least half the elements in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} are equal to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}}, an operation should not take long to complete because it will very quickly come across a \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}} entry. We shouldn't rely too heavily on this intuition, though, because it would lead us to (the incorrect) conclusion that the expected number of locations in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} examined by an operation is at most 2. For the rest of this section, we will assume that all hash values are independently and uniformly distributed in $\{0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}-1\}$. This is not a realistic assumption, but it will make it possible for us to analyze linear probing. Later in this section we will describe a method, called tabulation hashing, that produces a hash function that is ``good enough'' for linear probing. We will also assume that all indices into the positions of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} are taken modulo \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}, so that \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}} is really a shorthand for $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}\bmod\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}]$. \index{run} We say that a \emph{run of length $k$ that starts at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}} occurs when all the table entries $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}+1]}},\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}+k-1]$ are non-\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}} and $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}-1]=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}+k]=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}}$. The number of non-\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}} elements of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} is exactly \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} and the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} method ensures that, at all times, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}\le\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}/2$. There are \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} elements $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}}$ that have been inserted into \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} since the last \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} operation. By our assumption, each of these has a hash value, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{hash}}}}(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_j)$, that is uniform and independent of the rest. With this setup, we can prove the main lemma required to analyze linear probing.

content: \lemlabel{linear-probing} Fix a value $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}\in\{0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}-1\}$. Then the probability that a run of length $k$ starts at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} is $O(c^k)$ for some constant $0<c<1$.

If a run of length $k$ starts at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, then there are exactly $k$ elements $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_j$ such that $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{hash}}}}(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_j)\in\{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}},\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}+k-1\}$. The probability that this occurs is exactly \[ p_k = \binom{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}}{k}\left(\frac{k}{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}}\right)^k\left(\frac{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}-k}{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}}\right)^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}-k} \enspace , \] since, for each choice of $k$ elements, these $k$ elements must hash to one of the $k$ locations and the remaining $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}-k$ elements must hash to the other $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}-k$ table locations.\footnote{Note that $p_k$ is greater than the probability that a run of length $k$ starts at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, since the definition of $p_k$ does not include the requirement $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}-1]=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}+k]=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{nil}}}}$.} In the following derivation we will cheat a little and replace $r!$ with $(r/e)^r$. content: \thmlabel{linear-probing} A LinearHashTable implements the USet interface. Ignoring the cost of calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}}, a LinearHashTable supports the operations \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} in $O(1)$ expected time per operation. Furthermore, beginning with an empty LinearHashTable, any sequence of $m$ \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operations results in a total of $O(m)$ time spent during all calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}}.

\begin{thm}\thmlabel{linear-probing}
  A LinearHashTable implements the USet interface.  Ignoring the
  cost of calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}}, a LinearHashTable supports the operations
  \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}}, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} in $O(1)$ expected time per
  operation.  
  Furthermore, beginning with an empty LinearHashTable, any
  sequence of $m$ \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operations results in a total
  of $O(m)$ time spent during all calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}}.
\end{thm}

uniformly distributed over the set $\{0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{t}})}}-1\}$.  One way to
achieve this is to store a giant array, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{tab}}}}, of length $2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}$,
where each entry is a random \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}-bit integer, independent of all the

content: \index{hash code!for primitive data} Small primitive data types like \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{char}}}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{byte}}}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{int}}}}, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{float}}}} are usually easy to find hash codes for. These data types always have a binary representation and this binary representation usually consists of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}} or fewer bits.

content: In these cases, we just treat these bits as the representation of an integer in the range $\{0,\ldots,2^\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}-1\}$. If two values are different, they get different hash codes. If they are the same, they get the same hash code. A few primitive data types are made up of more than \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}} bits, usually $c\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}$ bits for some constant integer $c$. (Java's \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{long}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{double}}}} types are examples of this with $c=2$.) These data types can be treated as compound objects made of $c$ parts, as described in the next section.

content: \seclabel{stringhash} \index{hash code!for compound objects} For a compound object, we want to create a hash code by combining the individual hash codes of the object's constituent parts. This is not as easy as it sounds. Although one can find many hacks for this (for example, combining the hash codes with bitwise exclusive-or operations), many of these hacks turn out to be easy to foil (see Exercises~\ref{exc:hash-hack-first}--\ref{exc:hash-hack-last}). However, if one is willing to do arithmetic with $2\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}$ bits of precision, then there are simple and robust methods available. Suppose we have an object made up of several parts $P_0,\ldots,P_{r-1}$ whose hash codes are $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1}$.   \end{equation}
  since each of $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{z}}}}_i$ and $(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_i-\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_i)$ is at most $2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}-1$, so
  their product is at most $2^{2\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}-2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}+1}+1 < 2^{2\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}-1$.
  By assumption, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_i-\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_i\neq 0$, so \myeqref{bighash-xx} has at most one
  solution in $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{z}}}}_i$.  Therefore, since $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{z}}}}_i$ and $t$ are
  independent ($\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{z}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{z}}}}_{r-1}$ are mutually independent), the
  probability that we select $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{z}}}}_i$
  so that $h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1})=h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_{r-1})$ is at most
  $1/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}$.
  The final step of the hash function is to apply multiplicative hashing
  to reduce our $2\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}$-bit intermediate result $h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1})$ to
  a \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}-bit final result $h(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1})$.  By \thmref{multihash},
  if $h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1})\neq h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_{r-1})$, then
  $\Pr\{h(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1}) = h(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_{r-1})\} \le 2/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}$.
  To summarize, 
  \begin{align*}
    & \Pr\left\{\begin{array}{l}
          h(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1}) \\
          \quad = h(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_{r-1})\end{array}\right\} \\
      &= \Pr\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
            \mbox{$h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1}) = h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_{r-1})$ or} \\
            \mbox{$h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1}) \neq h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_{r-1})$} \\
                 \quad  \mbox{and
$\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{z}}}}h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}_{r-1})\ddiv2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}} = \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{z}}}} h'(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{y}}}}_{r-1})\ddiv 2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}}$}
          \end{array}\right\} \\
      &\le 1/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}} + 2/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}} = 3/2^{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}} \enspace . \qedhere
  \end{align*}
\end{proof}

content: Hash tables and hash codes represent an enormous and active field of research that is just touched upon in this chapter. The online Bibliography on Hashing \cite{hashing} \index{Bibliography on Hashing} contains nearly 2000 entries. A variety of different hash table implementations exist. The one described in \secref{hashtable} is known as \emph{hashing with chaining} \index{hashing with chaining} (each array entry contains a chain (List) of elements). Hashing with chaining dates back to an internal IBM memorandum authored by H. P. Luhn and dated January 1953. This memorandum also seems to be one of the earliest references to linked lists. \index{open addressing} An alternative to hashing with chaining is that used by \emph{open addressing} schemes, where all data is stored directly in an array. These schemes include the LinearHashTable structure of \secref{linearhashtable}. This idea was also proposed, independently, by a group at IBM in the 1950s. Open addressing schemes must deal with the problem of \emph{collision resolution}: \index{collision resolution} the case where two values hash to the same array location. Different strategies exist for collision resolution; these provide different performance guarantees and often require more sophisticated hash functions than the ones described here. Yet another category of hash table implementations are the so-called \emph{perfect hashing} methods. \index{perfect hashing} These are methods in which \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{find}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operations take $O(1)$ time in the worst-case. For static data sets, this can be accomplished by finding \emph{perfect hash functions} \index{perfect hash function} \index{hash function!perfect} for the data; these are functions that map each piece of data to a unique array location. For data that changes over time, perfect hashing methods include \emph{FKS two-level hash tables} \index{two-level hash table} \index{hash table!two-level} \cite{fks84,dkkmrt94} and \emph{cuckoo hashing} \cite{pr04}. \index{cuckoo hashing} \index{hash table!cuckoo} The hash functions presented in this chapter are probably among the most practical methods currently known that can be proven to work well for any set of data. Other provably good methods date back to the pioneering work of Carter and Wegman who introduced the notion of \emph{universal hashing} \index{universal hashing} \index{hashing!universal} and described several hash functions for different scenarios \cite{cw79}. Tabulation hashing, described in \secref{tabulation}, is due to Carter and Wegman \cite{cw79}, but its analysis, when applied to linear probing (and several other hash table schemes) is due to P\v{a}tra\c{s}cu and Thorup \cite{pt12}.   the HashTable or LinearHashTable implementations in this book,
  and design a program that stores integers in this data

  $c\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}$ elements that hash to the same table location.

content: Binary Trees
raw_latex: \chapter{Binary Trees}

content: \chaplabel{binarytrees} This chapter introduces one of the most fundamental structures in computer science: binary trees. The use of the word \emph{tree} \index{tree} \index{tree!binary} \index{binary tree} here comes from the fact that, when we draw them, the resultant drawing often resembles the trees found in a forest. There are many ways of ways of defining binary trees. Mathematically, a \emph{binary tree} is a connected, undirected, finite graph with no cycles, and no vertex of degree greater than three. For most computer science applications, binary trees are \emph{rooted:} \index{tree!rooted} \index{rooted tree} A special node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}, of degree at most two is called the \emph{root} of the tree. For every node, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}\neq \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}$, the second node on the path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} is called the \emph{parent} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. \index{parent} Each of the other nodes adjacent to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is called a \emph{child} \index{child} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. Most of the binary trees we are interested in are \emph{ordered}, \index{ordered tree} \index{tree!ordered} so we distinguish between the \emph{left child} and \emph{right child} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. \index{left child} \index{child!left} \index{right child} \index{child!right} In illustrations, binary trees are usually drawn from the root downward, with the root at the top of the drawing and the left and right children respectively given by left and right positions in the drawing (\figref{bintree-orientation}). For example, \figref{binary-tree}.a shows a binary tree with nine nodes.

content: Because binary trees are so important, a certain terminology has developed for them: The \emph{depth} \index{depth} of a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, in a binary tree is the length of the path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} to the root of the tree. If a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}, is on the path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}, then \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}} is called an \emph{ancestor} \index{ancestor} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} a \emph{descendant} \index{descendant} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}. The \emph{subtree} of a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, is the binary tree that is rooted at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} and contains all of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s descendants. The \emph{height} \index{height!in a tree} of a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, is the length of the longest path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} to one of its descendants. The \emph{height} of \index{height!of a tree} a tree is the height of its root. A node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, is a \emph{leaf} \index{leaf} if it has no children. We sometimes think of the tree as being augmented with \emph{external nodes}. Any node that does not have a left child has an external node as its left child, and, correspondingly, any node that does not have a right child has an external node as its right child (see \figref{binary-tree}.b). It is easy to verify, by induction, that a binary tree with $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\ge 1$ real nodes has $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}+1$ external nodes.

content: Using recursion this way produces very short, simple code, but it can also be problematic. The maximum depth of the recursion is given by the maximum depth of a node in the binary tree, i.e., the tree's height. If the height of the tree is very large, then this recursion could very well use more stack space than is available, causing a crash. To traverse a binary tree without recursion, you can use an algorithm that relies on where it came from to determine where it will go next. See \figref{bintree-traverse}. If we arrive at a node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{parent}}}}, then the next thing to do is to visit \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{left}}}}. If we arrive at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{left}}}}, then the next thing to do is to visit \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{right}}}}. If we arrive at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{right}}}}, then we are done visiting \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s subtree, and so we return to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{parent}}}}. \index{search path!in a binary search tree}%
The binary search tree property is extremely useful because it allows
us to quickly locate a value, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, in a binary search tree.  To do this we start
searching for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} at the root, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}.  When examining a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, there
are three cases:

content: \item If $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}< \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}$, then the search proceeds to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{left}}}}; \item If $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}> \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}$, then the search proceeds to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{right}}}}; \item If $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}= \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}$, then we have found the node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} containing \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}.

content: To add a new value, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, to a BinarySearchTree, we first search for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}. If we find it, then there is no need to insert it. Otherwise, we store \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} at a leaf child of the last node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}}}, encountered during the search for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}. Whether the new node is the left or right child of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}}} depends on the result of comparing \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}.
